newsitem.title: BELGIUM: HUNGARIAN THIRD IN BELGIUM'S VIOLIN COMPETITION.
newsitem.headline: HUNGARIAN THIRD IN BELGIUM'S VIOLIN COMPETITION.

text.p: Denmark's Nikolaj Znaider won Belgium's prestigious Queen Elisabeth violin competition in the early hours of Sunday with virtuoso renditions of Hofmeyr, Debussy and Sibelius.

Znaider, playing a 1704 Stradivarius, wins the use for four years of the Huggins Stradivarius violin, made in 1708 when the famed Italian violin maker was at what is considered to have been the height of his still-unfathomed creative mastery.
He also wins 500,000 francs ($17,000), concert bookings and recording sessions.
The Queen Elisabeth competition, which cycles every year in turn through violin, piano, composition and singing, was started in 1951 by the then Belgian Queen.

Imediately before the awards ceremony the 12 finalists filed on stage to perform together a brief piece written last week at the Queen Elisabeth music academy in Wateloo near Brussels, designed to show that despite their intense competition music still transcended boundaries.

Since Monday the finalists, picked over the past month from a field of 150 people from 34 countries, have mesmerised the audiences at Brussels' Fine Arts Palace and, through live television broadcasts, many in the rest of the country.
Of the finalists, two of whom have played each night from Monday to Saturday, Briton Andrew Haveron received the greatest audience and critical acclaim when he played on Thursday.
As usual, only six of the final dozen were chosen to receive special rewards as "laureates".
After Znaider, 21 years old, the second laureate of 400,000 francs ($13,000) and concert bookings went to Germany's Albert Breuninger for his renditions of Hofmeyr, Mendelsohn and Bartok.
Third was Hungary's Kristof Barati, who wins 350,000 francs ($12,000), followed by Haveron who wins 300,000 francs ($10,000).
Fifth was Japan's Natsumi Tamai who wins 250,000 francs ($8,000), and fellow Japanese Kazuhiro Takagi was the sixth laureate with a prize of 200,000 francs ($7,000).
Among this year's 14-person jury were famed classical violinists Yehudi Menuhin and Yfrah Neaman. REUTER 080123 GMT jun 97
